opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so nanochat is a small, end-to-end, hackable repo. You go from tokenizer training to pretraining to midtraining, SFT, a bit of RL, and then a little web UI where you can talk to your model. The whole thing fits in your head and runs on a single 8xH100 node in a few hours for a modest amount of money. What I find interesting is that this makes it a really nice sandbox, almost a fruit fly, for asking: can the models themselves improve this pipeline?

When people talk about recursive self-improvement, it can sound mystical. But concretely, a lot of what AI research is, at least the empirical part, is: look at a training run, form a hypothesis ("maybe the learning rate schedule is off," "maybe this data mixture is bad," "maybe we should change the architecture here"), make a change, run it, look at the loss and the evals, and iterate. That loop is extremely legible in something like nanochat. The metrics are clear, the runs are cheap enough, and the codebase is small enough that an agent can actually read all of it.

So the question becomes: if I hand this repo to a coding agent and say "make the CORE score go up for the same compute budget," how far does it get? My honest experience so far is that the models are useful but not autonomous researchers yet. They're great at boilerplate, refactoring, implementing a well-known idea when you point them at it. Where they struggle is the stuff that's off the data manifold. nanochat is intentionally written in a slightly unusual, minimal style, and the models keep trying to pull it back toward the standard internet way of doing things, adding defensive code, bloat, abstractions I don't want. They also don't have great taste about which experiments are worth running, and they'll sometimes convince themselves something worked when it's noise.

So I think of it less as "we're about to have a model that rewrites itself into superintelligence" and more as a measurable, small-scale benchmark for one part of the loop. You can literally track how much of the improvement on a speedrun-style leaderboard comes from humans versus agents over time. I'd expect that fraction to creep up gradually rather than suddenly flip. That's kind of my general view: this is more of a decade of slowly automating pieces of the work than a single moment where it takes off. But having a tiny, transparent pipeline where you can actually watch that happen is, I think, really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response describes nanochat as a small, transparent sandbox for testing whether models can improve its training pipeline, and asks how far a coding agent can get at improving it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that nanochat is a very small, very legible test bed, and recursive self-improvement is a very big, very fuzzy idea, and the interesting thing is what happens when you put them in the same room.

Nanochat is basically the full pipeline for a ChatGPT-style model in about eight thousand lines of code. Tokenizer, pretraining, midtraining, SFT, a bit of RL, evaluation, and a little web UI to talk to it. You can train the whole thing for around a hundred dollars on a single 8xH100 node in a few hours. The model you get is not smart. It's kind of like talking to a kindergartener. But every piece is there, and you can read all of it in an afternoon, and that's the point.

So why does that matter for self-improvement? Well, when people talk about recursive self-improvement, the thing they're really talking about is an agent that can look at the process that produced it, find something to change, and make the next version better. And if you try to do that on a frontier training stack, you're hopeless. It's millions of lines, it's distributed across thousands of GPUs, a single run costs tens of millions of dollars, and you get one shot. There's no loop to recurse on. Nanochat collapses that whole thing down to something where the loop is actually closable. You can hand it to an agent and say, here's the repo, here's the training script, here's the eval, make the number go up. And then run that overnight, and come back in the morning and see what it did.

And I think what you learn very quickly is that it's a lot harder than the science fiction version. The agent will do things like tweak the learning rate, change the warmup schedule, try a different tokenizer vocab size. Some of those work. Many of them don't. A lot of the time the gains are within noise, and the agent is very happy to declare victory on noise, so you have to be really disciplined about the eval. I actually think the eval is the whole game here. If the agent can measure improvement cheaply and reliably, the loop runs. If it can't, it just wanders.

The other thing you see is that the hard-won ideas in deep learning are not very compressible. The transformer architecture, the optimizer, the data mixture, these took the field years. A small model fumbling around with hyperparameters isn't going to rediscover that in an afternoon. So in practice I think of this less as "the model improves itself" and more as "the model becomes a reasonably good research intern on a very small problem." It can run experiments faster than I can. It doesn't get bored. But it needs a tight leash and a very good eval, and the ideas are still mostly coming from the human for now.

What I like about it as a research direction is that it's grounded. Instead of arguing about intelligence explosions on Twitter, you have an actual codebase, an actual compute budget, and an actual metric, and you can just watch what happens. And my prediction is that over the next couple of years those overnight runs get noticeably better, not because of some discontinuity, but because the models get a bit better at code, a bit better at not fooling themselves, and the tooling gets a bit better at letting them iterate. It'll feel like a slope, not a cliff. But a small repo you fully understand is, I think, exactly the right place to stand while you watch that slope.

r001.rationale: The response presents nanochat as a small test bed for exploring recursive self-improvement, describing an agent that changes the training process and measures whether the next model improves.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful thing about nanochat is that it makes the entire process small enough to experiment with. You have this loop of changing the code, training a model, evaluating it, and deciding whether the change helped. And you can start asking: how much of that loop can an existing model do autonomously?

I would distinguish that from a model directly rewriting its own intelligence. Initially, you're automating the work of the researcher. The model has some hypothesis about the training setup, modifies the experiment, looks at the results, and chooses what to try next. If it can do that reliably, then you have a mechanism that could improve the process used to train the next model.

The tricky part is deciding what counts as an improvement. You need a fixed compute budget, trustworthy evaluations, and enough experiments to distinguish a real gain from noise. Otherwise, the system can spend more compute or exploit some weakness in your measurement and appear to be making progress.

So I'd approach it as a very concrete experimental question: can an agent make a small GPT training recipe better, under controlled conditions? Then, if it succeeds, does that improvement transfer to a larger run? And eventually, does the resulting model become better at doing that research itself? That last step is where you actually start closing the recursive loop.

r001.rationale: The response presents nanochat as a controlled experimental setting for testing how much of GPT training and research an existing model can automate, including whether that can improve the next model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of nanochat as a way to make the entire process of training a GPT small enough that you can actually experiment with it end to end. You have the data, the pretraining, the post-training, the evaluations—all in one place. And that makes it an interesting environment for asking: how much of the research process can an AI do itself?

You could give an agent a fixed compute budget and say, “Here’s the code. Make the resulting model better.” It can change the architecture, the optimizer, the training recipe, run experiments, and look at the results. That’s already a loop where an AI is helping improve the process that produces AI.

But I’d distinguish that from a fully recursive self-improvement loop. If a very capable model is improving a much smaller model, you haven’t necessarily closed the loop. The interesting question is whether the improvements produce a system that is itself better at doing the next round of research.

And the hard part is making sure the progress is real. You need a trustworthy evaluation, you need to account for the compute spent searching, and you need experiments that finish quickly enough to get useful feedback. So I see it as a kind of laboratory: make the whole thing small, measurable, and easy to modify, and then see how much of that research loop you can hand over.

r001.rationale: The response presents nanochat as an end-to-end experimental environment for testing how much of the research process an AI can handle, including improving the model and the process that produces it.
